items.stem: Choose the best order for the lines: a. I am glad you liked it. b. Thanks for helping me choose it. c. Your presentation was excellent. d. The examples made the topic easy to understand. e. I spent all weekend preparing it.
items.expl: The order starts with the compliment, adds its reason, explains the preparation, and then gives the thanks and reply. The other orders break the conversation's logical sequence.

items.stem: Choose the best order for the lines: a. Finally, we tested the soil and planted native flowers. b. Our class wanted to improve the empty space behind the library. c. The librarian helped us design a small garden. d. We first removed litter and measured the area. e. The garden now attracts bees and makes the space brighter.

items.stem: Choose the best order for the lines: a. Please find the updated timetable attached. b. Dear students, c. The change affects the afternoon science classes. d. Thank you for your understanding. e. The laboratory will be closed on Tuesday for repairs.

items.stem: Choose the best order for the lines: a. That sounds useful. How can I join? b. Our neighborhood is starting a weekend repair club. c. You can register through the community website. d. Volunteers will fix small household items together. e. I have a broken lamp, so I would like to help.

items.stem: Choose the best order for the lines: a. The results showed that the new filter removed more plastic. b. We compared two water filters in our science project. c. Our teacher asked us to explain the difference. d. We recorded the amount of plastic after each test. e. We presented our findings to the class.

items.stem: Choose the best order for the lines: a. Finally, we emailed the report to the youth council. b. Our team wanted to compare traffic near two bus stops. c. We discussed the results and wrote three suggestions. d. First, we chose the stops and recorded traffic for one week. e. The report helped the council plan a safer crossing.

items.stem: Choose the best order for the lines: a. That sounds helpful. How can I reserve one? b. The library offers quiet study rooms after school. c. You can book a room at the front desk. d. items.stem: Choose the best order for the lines: a. I can bring labels and two large boxes. b. Our class needs to sort donated books. c. Let's meet in the activity room at four. d. The teacher asked us to prepare them for the community sale. e. We can separate children's books from reference books.

groups.title: Notice: Green Week Challenge
groups.passage:
GREEN WEEK CHALLENGE
Our school will hold a Green Week Challenge from Monday to Friday. Classes can reduce waste by bringing reusable bottles, sorting paper and plastic, and turning off lights when rooms are empty. On Friday afternoon, volunteers will clean the garden and record each class's results. The class with the highest score will receive a small library award. Students who cannot join the clean-up may submit a photograph of an eco-friendly action through the school website.

items.stem: The notice is mainly intended to ___ students to join an environmental challenge.
items.expl: The notice invites students to take part in Green Week. The other choices do not describe the purpose of the announcement.

items.stem: Students are encouraged to bring reusable ___.
items.expl: The passage specifically mentions reusable bottles. Lights, photographs, and awards are mentioned in different contexts.

items.stem: The garden clean-up will take place ___ Friday afternoon.
items.expl: We use on with a day such as Friday. At is used for a time, in for a longer period, and by gives a deadline.

items.stem: The class with the highest score will receive ___.
items.expl: The final sentence says that the highest-scoring class will receive a small library award. The other options are not prizes.

items.stem: Students who miss the clean-up can still take part by ___.
items.expl: The notice allows absent students to submit a photograph of an eco-friendly action. The other options do not express this alternative.

items.stem: The word reduce in the notice is closest in meaning to ___.
items.expl: To reduce waste means to use or create less waste. The other choices do not have the same meaning.

groups.title: Move More, Feel Better
groups.passage:
MOVE MORE, FEEL BETTER
A free health afternoon for teenagers
Saturday, 18 May | 2:00–5:00 p.m. | Riverside Youth Centre
Try a short dance class, learn how to plan a balanced snack, and speak with a nurse about healthy sleep. Wear comfortable clothes and bring a water bottle. Places in the dance class are limited, so register online before Thursday. The event is designed for beginners; no special fitness experience is required. Parents may attend the final fifteen-minute information session.

items.expl: The leaflet provides details about a free health afternoon for teenagers. It is not selling equipment or announcing an exam.

items.stem: The event is suitable for people who ___.

items.expl: Comfortable clothes are easy to wear without causing discomfort. The other choices do not match the meaning here.

groups.title: A Better Way to Recycle Phones
groups.passage: Many old phones are left in drawers even though they contain useful materials. Our school has started a phone-recycling project to collect unused devices. Students can bring phones to the office, where volunteers will remove personal data before sending them to a certified recycler. The project helps protect privacy and keeps electronic waste out of landfills. It also teaches students that a small action can support a more sustainable community.

items.stem: The project collects phones that are ___.
items.expl: The first sentence says that old phones are left in drawers, and the project collects unused devices. Certified describes the recycler, not the phones.

items.stem: Before recycling, volunteers will remove ___.
items.expl: Volunteers remove personal data to protect privacy. They do not remove the office or the landfill.

items.stem: The project helps keep electronic waste out of ___.
items.expl: The passage directly states that recycling keeps electronic waste out of landfills. The other places are not the intended answer.

items.stem: The project teaches students that a small action can ___.
items.expl: The final sentence says that a small action can support a more sustainable community. The other options are too broad or change the meaning.

items.stem: The word certified is closest in meaning to ___.
items.expl: A certified recycler is officially approved to do the work. The other choices describe ownership, location, or reuse, not approval.

groups.title: The Repair Club
groups.passage:
When a desk lamp stopped working, a student almost threw it away. A neighbor suggested taking it to the Saturday Repair Club at the public library. The club is run by volunteers who teach visitors how to fix small household objects instead of replacing them immediately. The student learned that a loose wire was the problem. With guidance, the student repaired the lamp and took it home that afternoon.

The club does not promise to repair every object. Volunteers first check whether an item can be fixed safely and whether the necessary tools are available. They also explain when a professional repair is needed. In addition to saving useful objects, the club gives residents a chance to share practical skills. The student now visits twice a month, not only to repair things but also to help younger visitors learn.

items.stem: What does the whole passage describe?
opts: Why desk lamps are difficult to use
A club that teaches people to repair objects
A volunteer's job at a school
items.expl: The passage explains how the Repair Club helps residents fix objects and share skills. The other choices are too narrow or unrelated.

items.stem: Why did the student take the lamp to the club?
opts: She wanted to buy a new tool
She wanted to throw it away
She wanted to learn whether it could be fixed
items.expl: The student first considered throwing the lamp away, but then took it to the club after receiving advice so the lamp could be fixed.

items.stem: What problem did the student find in the lamp?
items.expl: The passage directly identifies a loose wire as the cause of the lamp's problem.

items.stem: Volunteers check an object before repairing it in order to ___.
opts: decide whether repair is safe and possible
teach the owner a new language
items.expl: They check safety and tool availability before accepting an object. The other choices are not purposes mentioned in the passage.

items.stem: The word them in paragraph 1 refers to ___.
items.expl: In instead of replacing them, them refers to the small household objects that people bring to the club.

items.stem: What does the passage imply about the Repair Club?
opts: It accepts every object without checking it
It is useful only for professional engineers
It combines repair with community learning
It replaces the public library's normal services
items.expl: The club repairs objects and lets residents share practical skills, so it combines repair with learning. The other statements contradict the passage.

items.stem: Why does the student now visit twice a month?
opts: To repair objects and help younger visitors
To borrow a different lamp each week
items.expl: The final sentence gives both reasons: the student repairs things and helps younger visitors learn.

items.stem: Which statement is NOT true according to the passage?
opts: The student repaired the lamp with guidance.
The club guarantees that every object will be repaired.
The club meets at a public library.
items.expl: The passage says the club does not promise to repair every object, so the guarantee is not true. The other statements are supported.

groups.title: Restoring a Coastal Wetland
groups.passage:
For many years, a coastal wetland near a village became smaller as rubbish blocked its water channels and young trees were cut down. The wetland still protected nearby houses from some storm water, but its ability to support fish and birds was weakening. In 2022, local students began working with farmers, fishermen, and a conservation group to restore it.

The group first mapped the channels and recorded which areas held water during different tides. Students then collected rubbish and planted mangrove seedlings in places where the soil was suitable. Farmers helped build a simple path so visitors would not walk across new plants. After two rainy seasons, the wetland held water for longer, and more birds were seen there.

The project has not solved every problem. Some plastic still arrives from upstream, and the seedlings need protection. However, the work changed how residents viewed the wetland. Instead of seeing it as unused land, they now regard it as a natural barrier, a nursery for young fish, and an outdoor classroom for the village school.

items.stem: What change does the wetland project create?
opts: A village plan to build a new road
A competition between farmers and fishermen
A school trip to a distant island
A wetland restoration project and its benefits
items.expl: The passage describes how residents restored a coastal wetland and how the project benefited nature and the community.

items.stem: What had weakened the wetland before the project?
items.expl: The first paragraph identifies rubbish blocking the channels and the cutting of young trees as problems.

items.stem: Why did students map the channels?
opts: To choose a place for a classroom
To measure the height of the trees
items.expl: The group mapped channels and recorded areas holding water during different tides, so they could understand the wetland's water flow.

items.stem: Where were mangrove seedlings planted?
items.expl: The passage says that students planted seedlings in places where the soil was suitable.

items.stem: Why did farmers help build a path?
opts: To connect the wetland to an island
To carry fish to the market
To stop visitors walking on new plants
items.expl: The path kept visitors from walking across the new plants. The other options are not the reason given.

items.stem: What change was observed after two rainy seasons?
opts: The wetland held water longer and attracted more birds
The seedlings were moved to the school
items.expl: After two rainy seasons, the wetland held water for longer and more birds were seen there.

items.stem: The word it in paragraph 1 refers to ___.
items.expl: Its ability refers back to the wetland, which was becoming less able to support fish and birds.

items.stem: What problem remains after the project?
opts: Some plastic still comes from upstream
items.expl: The final paragraph says that some plastic still arrives from upstream and seedlings still need protection.

items.stem: How do residents view the wetland now?
opts: As land that should be sold
As a natural barrier and learning place
items.expl: Residents now see the wetland as a natural barrier, a fish nursery, and an outdoor classroom.

items.stem: Which title captures the wetland's change?
opts: From Unused Land to a Living Classroom
The Fastest Way to Build a Road
Why All Wetlands Should Be Closed
items.expl: The project changed the wetland from land residents ignored into a place that protects nature and supports learning.

Bring one broken item and a short note describing the problem. Put your name on the note so the volunteer can identify it. The service is free, although donations help buy tools. Visitors may watch the repair, learn a simple skill, and take the item home when it is safe. One item is accepted from each visitor.

groups.title: Learning Basic First Aid
groups.passage: The youth centre now offers a three-session course in basic first aid. A student enrolled after seeing a cyclist fall near a busy road and not knowing what to do. In the first session, the instructor teaches participants to check whether a scene is safe before helping. Later sessions cover calling emergency services, applying pressure to a small bleeding wound, and placing a breathing but unconscious person in a safe position. Participants practise with bandages and role-play cards, so they can make decisions without putting a real patient at risk. The instructor reminds the group that the course cannot replace professional medical care. Anyone who attends all three sessions receives a small wallet card showing that the course was completed.

groups.title: A Small Library Roof, A Larger Lesson
groups.passage: When the town library needed to reduce its electricity use, the staff considered putting solar panels on the flat roof. The first concern was whether the old roof was strong enough. Engineers inspected the structure and measured how much sunlight reached it during the day. After the inspection, a small set of panels was installed near the south side, leaving space for maintenance. A display in the entrance shows how much energy the panels produce each day. On cloudy days the amount is lower, but the panels still produce some electricity. Visitors can compare the display with the library's energy use and see why turning off unused lights matters. The system cannot power the entire building, and the library still buys electricity from the grid. However, the project has become a practical lesson about renewable energy. School groups now visit, ask questions, and record the changing output in their science notebooks.

items.stem: Why did the library consider installing solar panels?
opts: To close the building on cloudy days
To reduce electricity use and teach visitors
items.expl: The first sentence links the panels with reducing electricity use, and the passage later describes their teaching value.

items.stem: What was the first concern about the old roof?
opts: Whether it had a library display
Whether the panels could be painted
items.expl: The staff first needed to know whether the old roof could support the installation.

items.stem: What did engineers do before the installation?
opts: Inspected the structure and measured sunlight
Moved the library to another building
items.expl: Engineers inspected the roof structure and measured the sunlight it received.

items.stem: What can visitors see in the entrance?
opts: A map of every roof in town
A display showing daily panel output
A machine that stores all electricity
items.expl: The entrance display shows how much energy the panels produce each day.

items.stem: What happens on cloudy days?
opts: The panels produce a smaller amount of electricity
items.expl: The passage says that the output is lower on cloudy days, although the panels still produce some electricity.

items.stem: What can visitors learn by comparing the display with library use?
opts: How to build a complete roof
Why all buildings need to close
items.expl: The comparison helps visitors see why turning off unused lights matters.

items.stem: What limitation of the system is mentioned?
opts: It cannot power the entire building
It produces electricity only for visitors
It has no space for maintenance
items.expl: The passage says that the system cannot power the entire building, so the library still uses grid electricity.

items.stem: Why do school groups visit the library?
opts: To ask questions and record changing output
items.expl: School groups visit to ask questions and record the changing output in their science notebooks.

items.stem: What would be the best title for the library roof project?
opts: The Roof That Had to Be Removed
Why Clouds Stop All Solar Power
A Solar Project That Teaches the Community
items.expl: The project both produces some energy and gives visitors a practical lesson about renewable energy.

items.stem: What can be inferred about the library's approach?
opts: It plans to stop using the electricity grid immediately
It is interested only in decorating the roof
It uses data and a practical project to encourage careful energy use
items.expl: The display, energy comparisons, and school visits show an educational approach, although the library still uses grid electricity.
